s001.heard: A bank takes a hundred rupees from you. NCERT's example says it keeps twenty and lends eighty to someone else. You can still spend your hundred. The borrower can spend eighty. So there is now one hundred and eighty rupees to spend, where there was one hundred. Where did the extra eighty come from?

s002.heard: Last time we saw that, by M3, the broad measure, most of India's money is not cash. It is deposits. So who makes the deposits? And what stops them from growing without end?

s003.heard: We take it in four steps. A story NCERT tells. A bank's books. The limit, and the arithmetic of the limit. Then an honest question. Does the textbook picture match how banks work? This is part two of three.

s004.heard: NCERT tells the story of a goldsmith called Lala. Villagers leave their gold with him for safekeeping. He gives each a receipt. Slowly, the receipts themselves are used as money, because everyone in the village accepts them.

s005.heard: Then a man called Ramu asks Lala for a loan of twenty-five kilograms. Lala decides that not everyone will come for their gold at the same time. So he lends Ramu twenty-five kilograms of the hundred he holds. Ramu pays Ali with that gold, and Ali leaves it with Lala for a receipt. Now the receipts in use add up to one hundred and twenty-five kilograms.

s006.heard: It seems that Lala has created money out of thin air, says NCERT. It is a made-up story, not history. But NCERT says modern banks work the same way.

s007.heard: But Lala has a problem. If everyone came for their gold on the same day, he could not pay. NCERT says a bank can lend because it does not expect all depositors to withdraw together. But it must keep enough funds to repay any depositor on demand. Depositors stay only if they are fully confident of getting their money back.

s008.heard: To see the limit, read a bank's books. NCERT's balance sheet has two sides. Assets are what the bank holds, its reserves and its loans. Liabilities are what it owes, its deposits. Reserves are cash plus the bank's deposits with the Reserve Bank. Start with a bank that holds a hundred rupees of deposits and keeps all hundred as reserves. It has lent nothing yet.

s009.heard: Now the bank makes a loan. NCERT's answer is plain. It opens a new deposit in the borrower's name. So the money supply rises by that new deposit. In NCERT's example, the borrower's eighty rupees is such a deposit. And your hundred is still there. That is where the extra eighty came from.

s010.heard: So what stops a bank from lending without end? The first answer is a rule. NCERT says the Reserve Bank decides what share of deposits every bank must keep as reserves. This is the cash reserve ratio, the CRR. In the rules, that share is counted on a bank's net demand and time liabilities. It is kept as a balance with the Reserve Bank. NCERT says it is a legal requirement, meant to stop over-lending.

s011.heard: NCERT's example uses a reserve ratio of twenty percent. A hundred rupees is deposited. The bank keeps twenty and lends eighty. NCERT's example has only one bank, so the eighty comes back as a new deposit of eighty. The bank keeps sixteen and lends sixty-four. Round after round, the loans shrink by a fifth. Added up, deposits come to five hundred rupees, with reserves of one hundred and loans of four hundred.

s012.heard: Reserves of one hundred rupees created deposits of five hundred. NCERT calls the ratio the money multiplier. Here it is five. It is one divided by the reserve ratio. One divided by point two is five.

s013.heard: But people also keep some cash in their pockets. That cash leaks out of the process. The currency-deposit ratio is the cash people hold for each rupee of bank deposits. IGNOU counts demand deposits only. Here we count demand and time deposits together, as M3 does. IGNOU shows the multiplier is that ratio plus one, divided by that ratio plus the reserve ratio.

s014.heard: At the CRR of three percent on the third of November 2026, the plain formula gives thirty-three. In July 2026 the public held about fifteen paise of cash for every rupee of deposits. IGNOU's full formula then gives about six point four. Both are toy ceilings, not forecasts.

s015.heard: NCERT's Class 10 book says banks hold about five percent of deposits as cash. The legal minimum has since changed. On the third of November 2026, the CRR was three percent. It was four and a half percent until mid-December 2024, and four percent from the end of that month. Then, in four cuts of a quarter point in 2025, the Reserve Bank took it to three percent. The cuts ran from September to November.

s016.heard: Banks must also hold liquid assets, such as cash, gold and government securities. The minimum is eighteen percent of their net demand and time liabilities. That is the statutory liquidity ratio, the SLR.

s017.heard: The Reserve Ratio is one lever. NCERT says that when the Reserve Bank raises it, banks cut their lending, so the money supply falls. NCERT sorts the Reserve Bank's tools in two groups. Quantitative tools change the CRR, the bank rate, or buy and sell bonds. Qualitative tools include moral suasion and the margin requirement.

s018.heard: Take one tool. In an open market operation, the Reserve Bank buys a government bond and pays by cheque. That adds to the bank's reserves and to the money supply. Selling a bond does the opposite. And NCERT calls the Reserve Bank the lender of last resort. It stands ready to lend to banks at all times.

s019.heard: Now the honest question. Does a bank wait for reserves before it lends? Staff of the Bank of England wrote in 2014 about the modern economy. Most money, they said, is created by commercial banks making loans. Their article is about the UK. They said banks do not simply lend out the deposits savers leave with them. Nor do they multiply up central bank money. This was an article by Bank of England staff, in the Bank's Quarterly Bulletin.

s020.heard: Germany's central bank, the Bundesbank, said something similar in its Monthly Report of April 2017, about the euro area. A bank's ability to lend has nothing to do with whether it already holds excess reserves or deposits. Then what limits it? Its answer, the need to lend profitably, and the rules that regulate banks. Also what households and firms want to borrow and hold. And in normal times, the central bank influences the process through its interest rate policy.

s021.heard: Reserve rules are not universal. The United States cut its reserve requirement ratios to zero in March 2020. Yet NCERT and IGNOU still teach the multiplier.

s022.heard: IGNOU adds that in the real world the money supply is more likely a mix. It is partly controlled by the central bank, and partly shaped by firms, households and the banking sector. So when you write the exam answer, name the view you are describing.

s023.heard: The multiplier can also shrink. IGNOU recounts that in the United States, between March 1930 and March 1933, money fell about thirty-five percent. Over the same time, the monetary base rose about twenty percent. IGNOU gives two reasons. People pulled money out of banks, and banks held large excess reserves. IGNOU adds an argument. Friedman and Schwartz, among others, argued the fall was one of the major factors in the Depression. depression.

s024.heard: Which brings us back to confidence. One protection for a depositor is deposit insurance. Each depositor in a bank is insured up to five lakh rupees, for principal and interest together. The cover applies bank by bank, and the bank, not the depositor, pays the premium. The insurer says its aim is to secure public confidence in the banking system, particularly for the small depositor.

s025.heard: And how does a bank earn? It pays depositors less than it charges borrowers. The gap is called the spread. NCERT's Class 7 example, two hundred rupees lent at five percent brings ten rupees. Two hundred rupees deposited at two percent costs four. The bank earns six, before its own costs. On the third of November 2026, the Reserve Bank's rate panel showed savings deposits at two and a half percent. element.

s026.heard: For the exam, write it this way. A bank's loan opens a new deposit, so lending creates money. The limit in the textbook model is the reserve ratio. With a reserve ratio of twenty percent, the multiplier is five. Cash held by the public leaks out of the process, and the multiplier is smaller. On the third of November 2026, the Reserve Bank's CRR was three percent and the SLR eighteen. Name the view. The Bundesbank says lending is limited by profit, regulation and demand for credit. Bank of England staff name profit, regulation, the behaviour of money holders and monetary policy as the ultimate limit.

s027.heard: So, on NCERT's account, banks create money when they lend. Central-bank papers name limits such as profit and regulation.

s028.heard: But money is not the whole story of credit. Who gets a loan, at what price, and who is left out? In part three, credit in daily life, formal and informal, and how the money moves.
